title: Mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution
graph_title: Mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution
national_indicator_available: Mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution
national_indicator_description: This indicator measures the age-standardized mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution, also known as the burden of disease attributable to joint effects of household and ambient air pollution. Evidence from epidemiological studies have shown that exposure to air pollution is linked, among others, to the important diseases taken into account in this estimate: 1) Lower respiratory infections in general population; 2) Stroke in adults (25 years and over); 3) Ischaemic heart diseases in adults (25 years and over); 4) Chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases in adults (25 years and over); and 5) Trachea, bronchus and lung cancers in adults (25 years and over).
computation_definitions: Age-standardized rates adjust for differences in population age distribution by applying the observed age-specific mortality rates for each population to a standard population. The age-standardized rates can therefore be used to compare the rates of countries without being affected by the differences in age distribution from country to country.
computation_calculations: Death rates are calculated by dividing the number of deaths by the total population.
other_info: Estimates of mortality rate attributed to household and ambient air pollution are produced through a consultative and analytical process led by the World Health Organization (WHO) and are published annually.
comments_limitations: See linked data source for more information on methodology and limitations.

target_name: By 2030, substantially reduce the number of deaths and illnesses from hazardous chemicals and air, water and soil pollution and contamination
indicator_definintion: The mortality resulting from the exposure to ambient (outdoor) air pollution and household (indoor) air pollution from polluting fuels used for cooking and/or heating was assessed. Ambient air pollution results from emissions from industrial activity, households, cars and trucks which are complex mixtures of air pollutants, many of which are harmful to health. Of all these pollutants, fine particulate matter has the greatest effect on human health. By polluting fuels is understood kerosene, wood, coal, animal dung, charcoal, and crop wastes.
